sweep_summary: Both title-keyword items for gami1243 (Juskan 2015 'Selective accent revival in Liverpool'; De Lyon 1981 'A Sociolinguistic Study of Aspects of the Liverpool Accent') are about Scouse / Liverpool English and were attached to Yuwaalaraay-Gamilaraay by Glottolog's automated keyword match on 'Liverpool' (confirmed on both Glottolog reference pages and the JournaLIPP article page); neither concerns word stress in any Australian language, so relevance = other-language-or-variety, priority none, nothing fetched sources. the two open-access Giacon grammars (2014 thesis; 2017 Yaluu, APL 36) already on file from the 2026-09-16 audit were re-read: sec 2.9 (2017, pp.22-23) / sec 13.9 (2014, p.507) restate Williams 1980:27 and Austin 1993a — long vowels (and VG/VGV) always stressed, else initial primary stress, alternating secondary — which confirms the catalog's weight coding and adds refinements (VG/VGV count as long; -Vy final stress; purposive-form and reduplication exceptions). Catalog deciding source (Williams 1980) stands. written at

new_statements.quote: The acoustic realisation of stress has not been measured instrumentally, so the degree to which it is realised by pitch, loudness or length is not known. ... Stress rules have been given in Williams (1980: 27) and Austin (1993a). There are exceptions, but the great majority of words are covered by these rules: 1. Long vowels are stressed, even if in adjacent syllables; e.g. dháadháa 'grandfather'. For the purposes of stress, VG and VGV sequences count as a long vowel, e.g. ngíyaningùnda '1PL-LOC'. 2. If there is no long vowel, primary stress is on the first syllable, e.g. gába 'good'. 3. Secondary stress is on syllables two and four away from primary stress: gúmbulgàban 'turkey', bàluwáa 'slowly'.

new_statements.reading: Weight-sensitive (CVV heavy), unbounded: every long vowel (and vowel+glide sequences, which count as long) takes stress, even in adjacent syllables; with no long vowel, primary stress is initial; secondary stress alternates two and four syllables from the primary. Giacon adds first-hand refinements from the tapes: verb-final -Vy takes final stress (gubí-y, bumá-y), purposive forms of trisyllabic short-vowel stems often shift stress to the second syllable (bumáligù, wanaˈgigu), and some suffixed/reduplicated words (Gàmilaráay, màrrgamarrgáay) violate the rules; he flags word stress as 'not well described' (p.453). This CONFIRMS the catalog's 'weight' coding from Williams 1980 and refines it (VG/VGV count as heavy; purposive and -Vy exceptions). It does not supersede Williams 1980, which Giacon explicitly cites as the source of the rules and which was written from work with living speakers; Giacon 2017 is the corroborating newer reference grammar.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every clause of the deciding quotation and the p.33 ordering statement was found verbatim in the held Williams 1980 PDF at the stated pages (pp.26-27 text layer; p.33 page image). (2) The classification rests on a first-hand reference grammar with an explicit stress section and formal rules; the language has no L1 speakers and no instrumental or dedicated phonological study exists. The only newer grammar, Giacon 2017 (fetched sources now, open access, with), restates the same rules citing Williams and Austin 1993a and confirms the weight-sensitive, unbounded 'every long vowel stressed, else initial' coding (kind=weight, wcls=CVV, edge=unbounded, weight-blind alternating secondary). (3) Optional refinement, not a recode: Giacon 2017:22 adds 'VG and VGV sequences count as a long vowel' and verb-final -Vy str
